text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, for all you back pain sufferers, another pain reliever bites
the dust. So what's left, you might ask?

But there is a pain reliever which might be an effective treatment for depression,
although there could be a catch. Isn't there always?

An astounding one in 10 people will have a seizure during their life, some of them
will have epilepsy, but the definitions are changing.

And influenza. The flu season is almost upon us. We are being exhorted to be
immunised but how reliable is this year's flu vaccine? And should we be worried
about the deaths occurring in southern China at the moment from bird flu. They
do have the World Health Organisation worried because it's not just China,
there's a chicken cull on in Japan at the moment. Just in case it is safe to go out,
we thought we'd preview the flu season. And with me here in Melbourne to do
that is Dr Alan Hampson who chairs the Influenza Specialist Group. Welcome to
the Health Report Alan.

Alan Hampson: Good evening Norman.

Norman Swan: So what's in this year's vaccine?

Alan Hampson: There are four strains in this year's vaccine. We put in two
influenza A viruses, which are representative of two quite distinct subtypes of
influenza A. And there are two influenza B viruses. They are not as different, one
from the other, as if the influenza A viruses, but they represent two lines of
influenza B which have diverged since the 1980s.

Norman Swan: And is there much difference? Would you know whether you are
a hit with an A or a B, is B nastier than A or what?

Alan Hampson: It depends who you are I think. What we do tend to find is that
children are more affected by the influenza B viruses that adults, and adults,
particularly older adults, are more severely affected by one of the influenza A
viruses, the H3N2, but that pandemic virus which struck us in 2009, 2010…

Norman Swan: H5N1?
 
Alan Hampson: No, H1N1, it's still around. And it's still affecting younger adults
to a much greater degree than the other A virus does.

Norman Swan: And is that covered by the current set of vaccines?

Alan Hampson: Yes, it certainly is. In fact the strain that covers that has just
been updated this year in our vaccine.

Norman Swan: So how do you know which to put in?

Alan Hampson: It's a long process…

Norman Swan: It's better than roulette?

Alan Hampson: No, not quite. It's really based on surveillance, worldwide
surveillance through about 120 laboratories contributing to WHO's program. And
then twice a year now we have an evaluation of all the information that's
available.

Norman Swan: So these tend to be the viruses that are circulating in the
northern hemisphere that we expect to come down south?

Alan Hampson: It's a combination, because we also see viruses circulating
through the tropical areas out of those seasons.

Norman Swan: So if you go back to last year, which was a trivalent…I think it
was only three last year?

Alan Hampson: No, last year I think for the first time we did have a quadrivalent
vaccine, and the year before we had a trivalent vaccine.

Norman Swan: So how many were missed by the vaccine? How effective was
the vaccine relative to what actually hit Australia last year?

Alan Hampson: It was very close to the circulating strains. What we don't see
though is 100% protection unfortunately, that's a function of influenza vaccines,
the nature of the vaccines, but also the nature of the people who receive them.
Older people in particular we try to vaccinate. And as you get older your immune
system tends to wane, so we can't protect people as we might have been able to
when they were younger, and that's one of the reasons why we do try to
 
vaccinate people more widely, people who are in contact with high risk people
and people in the older age groups.

Norman Swan: So who should be immunised?

Alan Hampson: Well certainly anybody over the age of 65 should be immunised.
Anybody with a pre-existing risk condition, such as heart or lung disease, kidney
disease, diabetes, things of that nature, and pregnant women who are
particularly susceptible to the ill effects of influenza.

Norman Swan: But pregnant women and their GPs often think it's risky to have
an immunisation in pregnancy.

Alan Hampson: I think we are winning them round. They have thought that
vaccination was not good. GPs and obstetricians tend not to want to undertake
any treatment that is not absolutely necessary, but I think they are now seeing,
particularly in result of the 2009 pandemic where we saw a huge impact in
pregnant women, we are getting the message through now that it is both safe
and effective.

Norman Swan: So talking about effective, there's been a controversy about that.
Some people say it doesn't save the number of hospital bed days that it's
purported to, or indeed the number of lives. Is it effective?

Alan Hampson: It is effective, but it's not 100%. In fact the effectiveness may be
closer to 50% or 60%, and this is one of the reasons why the more people we
vaccinate, the greater the effect is going to be…

Norman Swan: Because you lower the amount of circulating flu.

Alan Hampson: That's right.

Norman Swan: And so tell us about what's going on in southern China. This
really toxic virus, its 40% mortality rate, which sounds terrifying, are we at risk?
What's going on? Is there another pandemic sitting there in the background?

Alan Hampson: We never know when a pandemic is going to arise. We've been
watching the H5 virus which has circulated more recently through the Middle
East but previously through Southeast Asia, that was the H5 virus…
 
Norman Swan: This one is called H7N9.

Alan Hampson: The new one is H7N9, it's only been circulating for about the
last five years in China. In a way it's more dangerous than the H5 virus…

Norman Swan: Because you can't pick it up in the chickens because they don't
get sick.

Alan Hampson: That's right, and the H5 virus you do see high death rates in the
birds, and we are still seeing that in parts of the world with the H5 virus.

Norman Swan: So what's not happening to make it a pandemic? Is this human
to human transmission?

Alan Hampson: Yes, we don't get any ongoing human to human transmission.
There might have been a rare case of human to human transmission, but the
virus has not yet acquired that ability. This has been the great fear for the last 15
years with the H5 virus, is that it will acquire that ability to spread, and it really
caused a lot of activity in terms of pandemic preparedness planning. The H7 has
come along and it looks a little more likely to be able to spread from person to
person, but it's still quite a way off being able to do that.

Norman Swan: Any coverage from the current vaccines?

Alan Hampson: No, none at all.

Norman Swan: So it may be safe to go out, who knows! Al Hampson, thanks for
joining us.

Alan Hampson: My pleasure Norman.

Norman Swan: Alan Hampson from the Influenza Specialist Group.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on RN, ABC news radio and CBC
radio across Canada. I'm Norman Swan.

Norman Swan: Most of us will have an episode of back pain at some time in our
lives, and sometimes the pain will radiate down one leg and be called sciatica,
and in a proportion of people that pain can last for weeks or months and can
involve weakness and numbness. Over the last couple of years the Health
 
Report has run stories on how paracetamol is pretty rubbish for back pain, as are
the so-called anti-inflammatories like Ibuprofen. These studies have emanated
from the George Institute in Sydney, and now a group of Australian and overseas
researchers have dug deeper and looked at a medication that is supposed to
target nerve pain to see whether that works, and they published their findings in
the current edition of the New England Journal of Medicine. The drug is called
pregabalin, the brand name is Lyrica, and Lyrica prescriptions have been
booming. But does it work for sciatica? Christine Lin of the George Institute is in
our Sydney studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Christine Lin: Thank you for having me Norman.

Norman Swan: So why would you think pregabalin would work, Lyrica would
work in back pain?

Christine Lin: We have some evidence that pregabalin works for other types of
nerve pain. And as you've already mentioned, that sciatica, which is often related
to the nerve roots coming out of our lower spine, is considered a type of nerve
pain. So we thought that pregabalin may be also effective for sciatica.

Norman Swan: And to what extent have prescriptions been booming?

Christine Lin: Just to give you an example, in Australia pregabalin the medicine
came onto the market, was approved by the Australian government for use of
nerve pain in 2013. And in 2014, 1.4 million scripts were written. In the next year
that number went up to 2.4 million, and that was 30% more than the government
originally predicted. And worldwide, pregabalin is actually the number one selling
drug for nerve pain.

Norman Swan: Gosh. And presumably it's not cheap.

Christine Lin: Yes, it does cost people money, and also it has side-effects, so
that's why we designed the study, to find out whether it's truly effective or not for
this patient population.

Norman Swan: So tell us about this study.

Christine Lin: So in this study we recruited more than 200 people who had at
least…who had sciatica of at least moderate if not severe intensity. These people
 
had pain that was bad enough for them to present to a GP for care, and when
they entered the study they were randomly given either the active or the placebo
medicine, and the patients were kept blinded as to which medicine they received
in order to keep the study as unbiased as possible.

Norman Swan: And presumably the doctors were blinded to it as well.

Christine Lin: Yes, the doctors, and also the other study personnel were also
blinded. And the patients…

Norman Swan: And so this was both acute sciatica and chronic, it lasted for a
while.

Christine Lin: That's right, so we recruited patients who had had at least one
week of pain, up to one year of pain. And these patients were put on the
medicine for up to 8 weeks, and the dose was adjusted for them according to
their progress by their doctor.

Norman Swan: And what were you looking for as outcomes?

Christine Lin: Our most important outcome was leg pain because that's the most
significant pain in a patient when they experience sciatica. And we collected the
outcome mainly at eight weeks, that was the main time point that we were
interested in, but we also followed the patients up over one year. And in addition
to leg pain we collected a range of other relevant clinical outcomes such as if
they had any back pain or if they were functioning okay.

Norman Swan: So what did you find?

Christine Lin: What we found was at eight weeks there was absolutely no
difference between the patients who took the active medicine compared to the
patients who took the placebo medicine in terms of how bad their leg pain was.
We also saw the same thing at one year, and this was also the same at eight
weeks and one year for all the other outcomes that we measured.

Norman Swan: What about side effects? Because it's not side-effect free.

Christine Lin: That's right, and that's the concern. And what we found was that
people who took the active medicine had nearly twice as many side-effects…
 
Norman Swan: Such as?

Christine Lin: Such as dizziness. Dizziness was actually the main side-effect.

Norman Swan: And you can get sedation with Lyrica too, can't you?

Christine Lin: Yes, I think so, dizziness and drowsiness. So the drug needs to
be carefully used in people operating heavy machinery or in elderly people.

Norman Swan: So does it work in other nerve pain? Why didn't it work in back
pain, if the nerves are involved in the sciatica?

Christine Lin: Well, there is some evidence that it works out for other types of
the back pain…

Norman Swan: Back pain or nerve pain?

Christine Lin: Sorry, other types of nerve pain. But one of the main reasons why
we think it hasn't worked for sciatica is that pain mechanism is a lot more
complex than we thought. So even though sciatica is considered a type of nerve
pain, there may be other mechanisms at play, including psychosocial factors.

Norman Swan: So explain more. But that's true of all pain. I mean, all pain is
affected by psychosocial factors; if you are feeling stressed, if you're depressed,
the pain can make you depressed. It's a very complex thing, pain, and back pain
is not alone in that. You know, chronic headaches, chronic arm pain, they all
have psychosocial factors. Pain is never simple.

Christine Lin: Yes, exactly, and so I think we are only beginning to understand
pain, and there's a lot more to be studied. But this also shows that we really need
to test each drug specifically for each patient's condition. So a drug that can work
for another pain condition may not be able to work for back pain or sciatica.

Norman Swan: Well, we are kind of running out here. We've found that
paracetamol is not much cop, paracetamol plus codeine is not much cop,
Ibuprofen and the anti-inflammatories are not much cop. You've got an epidemic
of opiate prescribing in the United States for things like chronic back pain and
sciatica, without much evidence that it does much more than just kill you. What's
left?
 
Christine Lin: Well, that's the problem. I think the picture is quite depressing in
terms of the treatment options. I think the most important thing is when people
have sciatica they are reassured that the pain will get better, and other than that
unfortunately we don't know…we don't have a good answer for what medicines
people can take in order to have them get better quicker.

Norman Swan: So have we shown that physio works, chiropractic, manipulation
of the back?

Christine Lin: Yes, for sciatica there's also unfortunately no convincing evidence
that other forms of…that physiotherapy works or other forms of physical
therapies work.

Norman Swan: And surgery is dubious. Although with sciatica there's probably
better evidence than just lower back pain.

Christine Lin: Yes, that's right, so for surgery there is evidence that surgery
works in selected patients over the short term, but after one year the results are
the same in people who haven't had surgery. So it is really up to the individual's
condition.

Norman Swan: What a cheery conversation Christine!

Christine Lin: Yeah!

Norman Swan: We look forward to your next trial which hopefully will find
something positive. But seriously though, thank you very much, a good trial and
in a great journal, thanks very much for joining us.

Christine Lin: Thanks Norman.

Norman Swan: Associate Professor Christine Lin of the George Institute for
Global Health in Sydney.

Norman Swan: Another painkiller is ketamine, it is used by ambulance officers in
cases of trauma because it doesn't lower blood pressure if you have a head
injury or you're bleeding, and it's also used in anaesthesia. Ketamine has also
unfortunately become a drug of abuse, but it is also known to help relieve
depression. The trouble is that has to be given by injection and it could be
 
dangerous if taken repeatedly, but that hasn't stopped doctors around the world,
including Australia, from prescribing it, which is why the Black Dog Institute in
Sydney is carrying out a trial of ketamine in people with depression, and one of
the investigators is with us now in our Sydney studio. Colleen Loo is Professor of
Psychiatry and director of the Sydney Neurostimulation Centre. Welcome to
the Health Report.

Colleen Loo: Hi Norman.

Norman Swan: So what is the evidence that ketamine helps depression?

Colleen Loo: Look, there's very good evidence, Norman, but mainly from studies
that have examined the effects of a single treatment. So we started with this
ourselves about five years ago in Sydney at the University of New South Wales,
and I must say that I was astounded by the results I saw, that people who were
highly treatment resistant, who were severely depressed, who had failed 10 or
more medications, could become completely well and free of depression within
24 hours of a single dose of ketamine.

Norman Swan: Given by intravenous infusion?

Colleen Loo: In that case we actually gave it by…so we actually trialled a few
things, an intravenous infusion, we also tried injecting it into the muscle or just
under the skin, and we've also tried actually sniffing the drug through the nose.
But whichever way you give it, it still seems to work quite well.

Norman Swan: How long for? Actually, before we come to how long for…in that
sort of situation that's when electroconvulsive therapy is used, ECT, to try and
get a quick response, particularly if people are suicidal and you really need to dig
them out of their deep depression. Has anybody compared it to ECT?

Colleen Loo: Yes indeed, there is a small study from overseas that has done
that, and remarkably it found that ketamine worked as well as ECT, but even
more quickly. I think that's preliminary and that still needs to be replicated and
there are now studies around the world doing that, but you're right, it's that
population that we are creating, people with barely severe treatment resistant
depression.
 
Norman Swan: And going back to that question before I so rudely interrupted
you, how long does it last for when you give one dose?

Colleen Loo: Well, that's the catch, Norman, and for a lot of people it doesn't
last, so you do tend to relapse back into your depressed state after a few days.
Curiously for some people…and we wrote up a case of someone we treated
where we gave a very small dose and she was actually well for five months, and
this was someone who had failed again on multiple medications. So that's one
things that we are still trying to understand and research, which people are going
to have what kind of response to ketamine.

Norman Swan: Tell me about this study you're doing.

Colleen Loo: One of the strategies that clinics in Australia and around the world
have started to use, because a single dose works so well, is, well, why not then
give repeated doses? And so they are doing exactly that. But the problem with
just giving repeated doses is we don't actually know how well does it work. So,
for example, will you keep having a good response, or will you actually start
having a kind of tolerance where after a while the drug doesn't work as well? And
how many doses should you give and how do you determine the dosing? And
also is it safe? You know, when you give a single treatment, yes, in the short
term you have passing side effects over the next hour or so, but when you give
repeated treatments then there are different implications for safety.

Norman Swan: So there are liver and bladder side-effects, isn't there?

Colleen Loo: So there are some potentially quite serious side-effects, and we
know of this mainly from knowledge in recreational drug users. This is one of the
problems, it hasn't been studied adequately under controlled conditions, but you
can get quite serious bladder problems where you actually get an inflammation or
even a kind of necrosis, a dying off of the lining of your bladder. This is not a
trivial problem because then…

Norman Swan: It doesn't sound like it!

Colleen Loo: You can get scar tissue and…

Norman Swan: It could make you depressed as well.
 
Colleen Loo: That's right. But it could then lead on to some permanent bladder
problems. This is something that is very important for people to be aware of. And
again, the studies looking at a single dose don't have this problem because it is
mainly an issue when you use it repeatedly. I'm told anecdotally that there is an
epidemic, for example, of bladder problems in places like Hong Kong where
there is a high rate of ketamine abuse.

Norman Swan: Are a lot of doctors using ketamine in Australia at the moment,
even though it's off label, they are not supposed to?

Colleen Loo: Yes, and 'off label' doesn't necessarily mean you're not supposed
to, just that it's not one of the indications that is published for the use of ketamine.
So there's an increasing interest in using ketamine, and colleagues do consult
me about it. The problem I think, Norman, is that we haven't yet worked out what
is the treatment protocol for using ketamine to treat depression, and does it work
with repeated dosing and is it safe? Or how do you need to use it for repeated
dosing for efficacy and safety?

And just to give you an example, there are cautionary tales published in the
literature case reports and also clinicians who have come to me where they've
had someone who is very treatment resistant, they have given them ketamine, it
works wonderfully the first time, then it wears off so they think, well, let's give
them a second dose. It doesn't work quite as well. And they fall into the trap of
giving people higher and higher doses and more and more frequently. Then after
a few weeks…

Norman Swan: So they're chasing it down a hole basically.

Colleen Loo: Exactly. And after a few weeks the person is right back where they
started, as depressed as when they started, but now they are receiving a
substantial does of ketamine every day, and then they worried about stopping
because the person might then rapidly deteriorate and become even worse. So
you've started with someone who was stably depressed, and then got caught in
that trap where you are giving them ketamine and they are just as bad as they
were, but if you stop they are likely to become even worse.

Norman Swan: It works in a different way from the usual antidepressant drugs,
can it be given with them and does it make them more effective?
 
Colleen Loo: Yes, in our trial that we are running, funded by the NHMRC, we
just have people on usually their stable doses of antidepressant medication, so
we give ketamine on top of that because there is no reason for stopping them,
but you're right, ketamine works on a different neurotransmitter system, different
chemicals in the brain, which is why it's a fascinating drug, and which probably
explains why it works so differently. You don't normally expect to see a rapid
response a day after starting an antidepressant medication.

Norman Swan: So briefly then, if somebody has got severe treatment resistant
depression and your doctor wants to give you a single dose of ketamine, that's
probably evidence-based but you're potentially getting into tiger country with
repeated doses and hold off until you know what the results of your trial is.

Colleen Loo: Exactly. So our trial is looking at the efficacy and safety of
repeated dosing. It looks at a four-week dosing protocol. It's a double-blind trial
but also with an open label treatment so that you can go on to have active
treatment. And I'm really interested beyond that in getting funding to look at what
a six-month treatment protocol should look like, because I think that's the ultimate
aim; how can we make this a clinically useful treatment?

Norman Swan: We'll book a slot for you to get the results on the Health Report.
Thanks for joining us Colleen.

Colleen Loo: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Professor Colleen Loo, who is Professor of Psychiatry at the
University of New South Wales and the Black Dog Institute.

Norman Swan: One in 200 Australian children live with epilepsy, four people in
100 will be diagnosed with epilepsy during their lives, and no doubt when you
hear the word epilepsy you think of a grand mal seizure where someone falls to
the ground, going stiff and blue and then jerking violently. But epilepsy is often far
more subtle and complicated and not always easy to diagnose and understand,
which makes it even more astounding that two-thirds of people labelled as having
epilepsy are not referred to an epilepsy specialist. All these are among the
reasons that the way the different types of epilepsy should be classified has had
its first revision in 30 years. One of the experts behind this is Professor Ingrid
Scheffer who is a paediatric neurologist and epileptologist at the University of
 
Melbourne, and co-winner of the Prime Minister's Science Prize in 2014 for her
work on epilepsy. Welcome Ingrid.

Ingrid Scheffer: Thank you very much, Norman.

Norman Swan: So suffice it to say this is complicated, we don't have three
years, we have about seven minutes. Just tell us, why the reclassification and
what's the net effect of it?

Ingrid Scheffer: Well, it was a desperate need to bring it up to date. Science has
moved on, epilepsy has moved on since 1989 and we needed to bring in their
new concepts to how we look at patients, how we make diagnoses, how we look
for causes, very importantly, and that of course influences treatment. So it was
very timely, but it is complex. And as Einstein said, it should be as simple as
possible but no simpler, and that was something we really struggled with, was
trying to get it so that it was using words that mean what they say and would be
something that patients could use, doctors could use and everyone around them.

Norman Swan: And you say in your paper that the science is not yet up to a
proper classification, that you can't classify it like cancer or diabetes, so you just
take a practical approach, an operational approach rather than a science-based
approach.

Ingrid Scheffer: Yes, but there's a lot more science informing it now than 30
years ago, and that of course will change dramatically in the next 10 or 20 years.

Norman Swan: So take us through some of the big changes.

Ingrid Scheffer: Well, I think the big changes are the framework for how we
approach…when you see somebody with their first seizure or in fact epilepsy if
it's uncontrolled, and first you want to know the type of seizure they have, so we
have a whole new framework of new terms for seizures which are meant to be
more transparent. And then we take them up to try to diagnose their epilepsy
type, and ideally their epilepsy syndrome. You can't always make a syndrome
diagnosis.

Norman Swan: By syndrome you mean what?
 
Ingrid Scheffer: By syndrome I mean types of seizures that might occur
together. So people will often have three or four different types of seizures and
you need to know what goes with what. And then the EEG or the brainwave
tracing, what that shows, and then maybe the MRI as well, and you put that all
together to make an epilepsy syndrome diagnosis. And a good example is
childhood absence epilepsy, where a child stops and stares.

Norman Swan: So take us through the classical types of epileptic seizures or fits
and what they look like and how it changes.

Ingrid Scheffer: Okay, well, the seizure types don't change, but the words have
improved. So you have two big groups where they begin in one part of the brain
which were called partial and are now called focal. And in focal seizures, which
are 60% of all epilepsy, so the biggest group, you can be with it, which we call an
aware seizure now…

Norman Swan: So you know you are having it.

Ingrid Scheffer: Exactly.

Norman Swan: Which when I was a medical student that told you it wasn't
epilepsy at all but now we know it is.

Ingrid Scheffer: Exactly. And now impaired awareness. So instead of what was
complex partial, and complex doesn't mean not knowing where you are but
impaired awareness does, so now it's focal impaired awareness seizure. That's
diagnosis is critical, if you have it you can't drive, so it's a really important one for
our society.

Norman Swan: So it has an impact. And these focal epilepsies, they can be an
unusual behaviour, you stand up and walk to the end of the room and you don't
know where you are when you come round.

Ingrid Scheffer: Exactly, so you can just be a bit confused, 'off the air' we often
say, you might look to one side, you might go pale, you might do nothing, it can
be really boring to look at.

Norman Swan: So in the old days this was what was called petit mal, is it?
 
Ingrid Scheffer: Well, that's the problem with the French, everyone loves the
petit mal and the grand mal, but in fact they meant a host of different seizure
types, so they went out in 1981.

Norman Swan: All right, that shows how up-to-date I am.

Ingrid Scheffer: And we've now been working on these other ones. So there's a
focal group, and then the other big group are the generalised groups, which start
in both sides of the brain at once and involve the old grand mal means tonic
clonic, where you go stiff, tonic, and clonic, jerking, so stiffen and jerking, and
you fall to the ground with loss of consciousness. And the other main well-known
ones are absence, so you stop and stare, often just for five seconds and then
you are back with it. And the third big one is the myoclonic seizure where you
jerk.

Norman Swan: So then go down a level, so that's, if you like, exactly what is
happening to you and describing it for what it is. The causes…the reason you
and Sam Berkovic got the PM's Science Prize was for your work on the genetics
of this.

Ingrid Scheffer: Exactly, so the causes are now up front and centre. From the
moment you see somebody with a seizure you have to ask yourself what's the
cause. And when we started in what we are doing there were no genes known
for epilepsy, we found the first one in 1995 with John Mulley from Adelaide. And
that really has made…genetics has since come to the fore with new next-
generation sequencing techniques, the new gene finding science, and we now
have about 400 genes known for epilepsy, so there are many.

Norman Swan: Mostly in childhood epilepsy or first seizure in adults? Because
the first seizure in adults the alarm bells ring; does this person have a malignant
tumour, for example, what's going on here?

Ingrid Scheffer: So more in childhood and adolescent onset, but some adults
can have genetic forms as well. And they may have malformations, and we know
that there are subtle malformations of the brain that cause focal epilepsies, but
there's a whole host of other causes that we now think about, including structural
changes and metabolic changes.
 
Norman Swan: Where can people go to find out more?

Ingrid Scheffer: Well, the International League Against Epilepsy is the
international body that defines epilepsy, and this is like the DSM5, if you like,
which is for psychiatry but the equivalent for epilepsy, and so you can look at
their website to get more information.

Norman Swan: And get a referral to an epileptologist rather than sticking with
the doctor who doesn't necessarily…

Ingrid Scheffer: Oh I think lots of paediatricians and neurologists are very
capable with epilepsy, so they'd be perfectly good too.

Norman Swan: Ingrid Scheffer, thanks for joining us.

Ingrid Scheffer: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Professor Ingrid Scheffer is a paediatric neurologist and
epileptoloist at the University of Melbourne.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report, and I hope you can join me
next week.

pages.text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, for all you back pain sufferers, another pain reliever bites
the dust. So what's left, you might ask?

But there is a pain reliever which might be an effective treatment for depression,
although there could be a catch. Isn't there always?

An astounding one in 10 people will have a seizure during their life, some of them
will have epilepsy, but the definitions are changing.

And influenza. The flu season is almost upon us. We are being exhorted to be
immunised but how reliable is this year's flu vaccine? And should we be worried
about the deaths occurring in southern China at the moment from bird flu. They
do have the World Health Organisation worried because it's not just China,
there's a chicken cull on in Japan at the moment. Just in case it is safe to go out,
we thought we'd preview the flu season. And with me here in Melbourne to do
that is Dr Alan Hampson who chairs the Influenza Specialist Group. Welcome to
the Health Report Alan.

Alan Hampson: Good evening Norman.

Norman Swan: So what's in this year's vaccine?

Alan Hampson: There are four strains in this year's vaccine. We put in two
influenza A viruses, which are representative of two quite distinct subtypes of
influenza A. And there are two influenza B viruses. They are not as different, one
from the other, as if the influenza A viruses, but they represent two lines of
influenza B which have diverged since the 1980s.

Norman Swan: And is there much difference? Would you know whether you are
a hit with an A or a B, is B nastier than A or what?

Alan Hampson: It depends who you are I think. What we do tend to find is that
children are more affected by the influenza B viruses that adults, and adults,
particularly older adults, are more severely affected by one of the influenza A
viruses, the H3N2, but that pandemic virus which struck us in 2009, 2010…

Norman Swan: H5N1?

Alan Hampson: No, H1N1, it's still around. And it's still affecting younger adults
to a much greater degree than the other A virus does.

Norman Swan: And is that covered by the current set of vaccines?

Alan Hampson: Yes, it certainly is. In fact the strain that covers that has just
been updated this year in our vaccine.

Norman Swan: So how do you know which to put in?

Alan Hampson: It's a long process…

Norman Swan: It's better than roulette?

Alan Hampson: No, not quite. It's really based on surveillance, worldwide
surveillance through about 120 laboratories contributing to WHO's program. And
then twice a year now we have an evaluation of all the information that's
available.

Norman Swan: So these tend to be the viruses that are circulating in the
northern hemisphere that we expect to come down south?

Alan Hampson: It's a combination, because we also see viruses circulating
through the tropical areas out of those seasons.

Norman Swan: So if you go back to last year, which was a trivalent…I think it
was only three last year?

Alan Hampson: No, last year I think for the first time we did have a quadrivalent
vaccine, and the year before we had a trivalent vaccine.

Norman Swan: So how many were missed by the vaccine? How effective was
the vaccine relative to what actually hit Australia last year?

Alan Hampson: It was very close to the circulating strains. What we don't see
though is 100% protection unfortunately, that's a function of influenza vaccines,
the nature of the vaccines, but also the nature of the people who receive them.
Older people in particular we try to vaccinate. And as you get older your immune
system tends to wane, so we can't protect people as we might have been able to
when they were younger, and that's one of the reasons why we do try to

vaccinate people more widely, people who are in contact with high risk people
and people in the older age groups.

Norman Swan: So who should be immunised?

Alan Hampson: Well certainly anybody over the age of 65 should be immunised.
Anybody with a pre-existing risk condition, such as heart or lung disease, kidney
disease, diabetes, things of that nature, and pregnant women who are
particularly susceptible to the ill effects of influenza.

Norman Swan: But pregnant women and their GPs often think it's risky to have
an immunisation in pregnancy.

Alan Hampson: I think we are winning them round. They have thought that
vaccination was not good. GPs and obstetricians tend not to want to undertake
any treatment that is not absolutely necessary, but I think they are now seeing,
particularly in result of the 2009 pandemic where we saw a huge impact in
pregnant women, we are getting the message through now that it is both safe
and effective.

Norman Swan: So talking about effective, there's been a controversy about that.
Some people say it doesn't save the number of hospital bed days that it's
purported to, or indeed the number of lives. Is it effective?

Alan Hampson: It is effective, but it's not 100%. In fact the effectiveness may be
closer to 50% or 60%, and this is one of the reasons why the more people we
vaccinate, the greater the effect is going to be…

Norman Swan: Because you lower the amount of circulating flu.

Alan Hampson: That's right.

Norman Swan: And so tell us about what's going on in southern China. This
really toxic virus, its 40% mortality rate, which sounds terrifying, are we at risk?
What's going on? Is there another pandemic sitting there in the background?

Alan Hampson: We never know when a pandemic is going to arise. We've been
watching the H5 virus which has circulated more recently through the Middle
East but previously through Southeast Asia, that was the H5 virus…

Norman Swan: This one is called H7N9.

Alan Hampson: The new one is H7N9, it's only been circulating for about the
last five years in China. In a way it's more dangerous than the H5 virus…

Norman Swan: Because you can't pick it up in the chickens because they don't
get sick.

Alan Hampson: That's right, and the H5 virus you do see high death rates in the
birds, and we are still seeing that in parts of the world with the H5 virus.

Norman Swan: So what's not happening to make it a pandemic? Is this human
to human transmission?

Alan Hampson: Yes, we don't get any ongoing human to human transmission.
There might have been a rare case of human to human transmission, but the
virus has not yet acquired that ability. This has been the great fear for the last 15
years with the H5 virus, is that it will acquire that ability to spread, and it really
caused a lot of activity in terms of pandemic preparedness planning. The H7 has
come along and it looks a little more likely to be able to spread from person to
person, but it's still quite a way off being able to do that.

Norman Swan: Any coverage from the current vaccines?

Alan Hampson: No, none at all.

Norman Swan: So it may be safe to go out, who knows! Al Hampson, thanks for
joining us.

Alan Hampson: My pleasure Norman.

Norman Swan: Alan Hampson from the Influenza Specialist Group.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on RN, ABC news radio and CBC
radio across Canada. I'm Norman Swan.

Norman Swan: Most of us will have an episode of back pain at some time in our
lives, and sometimes the pain will radiate down one leg and be called sciatica,
and in a proportion of people that pain can last for weeks or months and can
involve weakness and numbness. Over the last couple of years the Health

Report has run stories on how paracetamol is pretty rubbish for back pain, as are
the so-called anti-inflammatories like Ibuprofen. These studies have emanated
from the George Institute in Sydney, and now a group of Australian and overseas
researchers have dug deeper and looked at a medication that is supposed to
target nerve pain to see whether that works, and they published their findings in
the current edition of the New England Journal of Medicine. The drug is called
pregabalin, the brand name is Lyrica, and Lyrica prescriptions have been
booming. But does it work for sciatica? Christine Lin of the George Institute is in
our Sydney studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Christine Lin: Thank you for having me Norman.

Norman Swan: So why would you think pregabalin would work, Lyrica would
work in back pain?

Christine Lin: We have some evidence that pregabalin works for other types of
nerve pain. And as you've already mentioned, that sciatica, which is often related
to the nerve roots coming out of our lower spine, is considered a type of nerve
pain. So we thought that pregabalin may be also effective for sciatica.

Norman Swan: And to what extent have prescriptions been booming?

Christine Lin: Just to give you an example, in Australia pregabalin the medicine
came onto the market, was approved by the Australian government for use of
nerve pain in 2013. And in 2014, 1.4 million scripts were written. In the next year
that number went up to 2.4 million, and that was 30% more than the government
originally predicted. And worldwide, pregabalin is actually the number one selling
drug for nerve pain.

Norman Swan: Gosh. And presumably it's not cheap.

Christine Lin: Yes, it does cost people money, and also it has side-effects, so
that's why we designed the study, to find out whether it's truly effective or not for
this patient population.

Norman Swan: So tell us about this study.

Christine Lin: So in this study we recruited more than 200 people who had at
least…who had sciatica of at least moderate if not severe intensity. These people

had pain that was bad enough for them to present to a GP for care, and when
they entered the study they were randomly given either the active or the placebo
medicine, and the patients were kept blinded as to which medicine they received
in order to keep the study as unbiased as possible.

Norman Swan: And presumably the doctors were blinded to it as well.

Christine Lin: Yes, the doctors, and also the other study personnel were also
blinded. And the patients…

Norman Swan: And so this was both acute sciatica and chronic, it lasted for a
while.

Christine Lin: That's right, so we recruited patients who had had at least one
week of pain, up to one year of pain. And these patients were put on the
medicine for up to 8 weeks, and the dose was adjusted for them according to
their progress by their doctor.

Norman Swan: And what were you looking for as outcomes?

Christine Lin: Our most important outcome was leg pain because that's the most
significant pain in a patient when they experience sciatica. And we collected the
outcome mainly at eight weeks, that was the main time point that we were
interested in, but we also followed the patients up over one year. And in addition
to leg pain we collected a range of other relevant clinical outcomes such as if
they had any back pain or if they were functioning okay.

Norman Swan: So what did you find?

Christine Lin: What we found was at eight weeks there was absolutely no
difference between the patients who took the active medicine compared to the
patients who took the placebo medicine in terms of how bad their leg pain was.
We also saw the same thing at one year, and this was also the same at eight
weeks and one year for all the other outcomes that we measured.

Norman Swan: What about side effects? Because it's not side-effect free.

Christine Lin: That's right, and that's the concern. And what we found was that
people who took the active medicine had nearly twice as many side-effects…

Norman Swan: Such as?

Christine Lin: Such as dizziness. Dizziness was actually the main side-effect.

Norman Swan: And you can get sedation with Lyrica too, can't you?

Christine Lin: Yes, I think so, dizziness and drowsiness. So the drug needs to
be carefully used in people operating heavy machinery or in elderly people.

Norman Swan: So does it work in other nerve pain? Why didn't it work in back
pain, if the nerves are involved in the sciatica?

Christine Lin: Well, there is some evidence that it works out for other types of
the back pain…

Norman Swan: Back pain or nerve pain?

Christine Lin: Sorry, other types of nerve pain. But one of the main reasons why
we think it hasn't worked for sciatica is that pain mechanism is a lot more
complex than we thought. So even though sciatica is considered a type of nerve
pain, there may be other mechanisms at play, including psychosocial factors.

Norman Swan: So explain more. But that's true of all pain. I mean, all pain is
affected by psychosocial factors; if you are feeling stressed, if you're depressed,
the pain can make you depressed. It's a very complex thing, pain, and back pain
is not alone in that. You know, chronic headaches, chronic arm pain, they all
have psychosocial factors. Pain is never simple.

Christine Lin: Yes, exactly, and so I think we are only beginning to understand
pain, and there's a lot more to be studied. But this also shows that we really need
to test each drug specifically for each patient's condition. So a drug that can work
for another pain condition may not be able to work for back pain or sciatica.

Norman Swan: Well, we are kind of running out here. We've found that
paracetamol is not much cop, paracetamol plus codeine is not much cop,
Ibuprofen and the anti-inflammatories are not much cop. You've got an epidemic
of opiate prescribing in the United States for things like chronic back pain and
sciatica, without much evidence that it does much more than just kill you. What's
left?

Christine Lin: Well, that's the problem. I think the picture is quite depressing in
terms of the treatment options. I think the most important thing is when people
have sciatica they are reassured that the pain will get better, and other than that
unfortunately we don't know…we don't have a good answer for what medicines
people can take in order to have them get better quicker.

Norman Swan: So have we shown that physio works, chiropractic, manipulation
of the back?

Christine Lin: Yes, for sciatica there's also unfortunately no convincing evidence
that other forms of…that physiotherapy works or other forms of physical
therapies work.

Norman Swan: And surgery is dubious. Although with sciatica there's probably
better evidence than just lower back pain.

Christine Lin: Yes, that's right, so for surgery there is evidence that surgery
works in selected patients over the short term, but after one year the results are
the same in people who haven't had surgery. So it is really up to the individual's
condition.

Norman Swan: What a cheery conversation Christine!

Christine Lin: Yeah!

Norman Swan: We look forward to your next trial which hopefully will find
something positive. But seriously though, thank you very much, a good trial and
in a great journal, thanks very much for joining us.

Christine Lin: Thanks Norman.

Norman Swan: Associate Professor Christine Lin of the George Institute for
Global Health in Sydney.

Norman Swan: Another painkiller is ketamine, it is used by ambulance officers in
cases of trauma because it doesn't lower blood pressure if you have a head
injury or you're bleeding, and it's also used in anaesthesia. Ketamine has also
unfortunately become a drug of abuse, but it is also known to help relieve
depression. The trouble is that has to be given by injection and it could be

dangerous if taken repeatedly, but that hasn't stopped doctors around the world,
including Australia, from prescribing it, which is why the Black Dog Institute in
Sydney is carrying out a trial of ketamine in people with depression, and one of
the investigators is with us now in our Sydney studio. Colleen Loo is Professor of
Psychiatry and director of the Sydney Neurostimulation Centre. Welcome to
the Health Report.

Colleen Loo: Hi Norman.

Norman Swan: So what is the evidence that ketamine helps depression?

Colleen Loo: Look, there's very good evidence, Norman, but mainly from studies
that have examined the effects of a single treatment. So we started with this
ourselves about five years ago in Sydney at the University of New South Wales,
and I must say that I was astounded by the results I saw, that people who were
highly treatment resistant, who were severely depressed, who had failed 10 or
more medications, could become completely well and free of depression within
24 hours of a single dose of ketamine.

Norman Swan: Given by intravenous infusion?

Colleen Loo: In that case we actually gave it by…so we actually trialled a few
things, an intravenous infusion, we also tried injecting it into the muscle or just
under the skin, and we've also tried actually sniffing the drug through the nose.
But whichever way you give it, it still seems to work quite well.

Norman Swan: How long for? Actually, before we come to how long for…in that
sort of situation that's when electroconvulsive therapy is used, ECT, to try and
get a quick response, particularly if people are suicidal and you really need to dig
them out of their deep depression. Has anybody compared it to ECT?

Colleen Loo: Yes indeed, there is a small study from overseas that has done
that, and remarkably it found that ketamine worked as well as ECT, but even
more quickly. I think that's preliminary and that still needs to be replicated and
there are now studies around the world doing that, but you're right, it's that
population that we are creating, people with barely severe treatment resistant
depression.

Norman Swan: And going back to that question before I so rudely interrupted
you, how long does it last for when you give one dose?

Colleen Loo: Well, that's the catch, Norman, and for a lot of people it doesn't
last, so you do tend to relapse back into your depressed state after a few days.
Curiously for some people…and we wrote up a case of someone we treated
where we gave a very small dose and she was actually well for five months, and
this was someone who had failed again on multiple medications. So that's one
things that we are still trying to understand and research, which people are going
to have what kind of response to ketamine.

Norman Swan: Tell me about this study you're doing.

Colleen Loo: One of the strategies that clinics in Australia and around the world
have started to use, because a single dose works so well, is, well, why not then
give repeated doses? And so they are doing exactly that. But the problem with
just giving repeated doses is we don't actually know how well does it work. So,
for example, will you keep having a good response, or will you actually start
having a kind of tolerance where after a while the drug doesn't work as well? And
how many doses should you give and how do you determine the dosing? And
also is it safe? You know, when you give a single treatment, yes, in the short
term you have passing side effects over the next hour or so, but when you give
repeated treatments then there are different implications for safety.

Norman Swan: So there are liver and bladder side-effects, isn't there?

Colleen Loo: So there are some potentially quite serious side-effects, and we
know of this mainly from knowledge in recreational drug users. This is one of the
problems, it hasn't been studied adequately under controlled conditions, but you
can get quite serious bladder problems where you actually get an inflammation or
even a kind of necrosis, a dying off of the lining of your bladder. This is not a
trivial problem because then…

Norman Swan: It doesn't sound like it!

Colleen Loo: You can get scar tissue and…

Norman Swan: It could make you depressed as well.

Colleen Loo: That's right. But it could then lead on to some permanent bladder
problems. This is something that is very important for people to be aware of. And
again, the studies looking at a single dose don't have this problem because it is
mainly an issue when you use it repeatedly. I'm told anecdotally that there is an
epidemic, for example, of bladder problems in places like Hong Kong where
there is a high rate of ketamine abuse.

Norman Swan: Are a lot of doctors using ketamine in Australia at the moment,
even though it's off label, they are not supposed to?

Colleen Loo: Yes, and 'off label' doesn't necessarily mean you're not supposed
to, just that it's not one of the indications that is published for the use of ketamine.
So there's an increasing interest in using ketamine, and colleagues do consult
me about it. The problem I think, Norman, is that we haven't yet worked out what
is the treatment protocol for using ketamine to treat depression, and does it work
with repeated dosing and is it safe? Or how do you need to use it for repeated
dosing for efficacy and safety?

And just to give you an example, there are cautionary tales published in the
literature case reports and also clinicians who have come to me where they've
had someone who is very treatment resistant, they have given them ketamine, it
works wonderfully the first time, then it wears off so they think, well, let's give
them a second dose. It doesn't work quite as well. And they fall into the trap of
giving people higher and higher doses and more and more frequently. Then after
a few weeks…

Norman Swan: So they're chasing it down a hole basically.

Colleen Loo: Exactly. And after a few weeks the person is right back where they
started, as depressed as when they started, but now they are receiving a
substantial does of ketamine every day, and then they worried about stopping
because the person might then rapidly deteriorate and become even worse. So
you've started with someone who was stably depressed, and then got caught in
that trap where you are giving them ketamine and they are just as bad as they
were, but if you stop they are likely to become even worse.

Norman Swan: It works in a different way from the usual antidepressant drugs,
can it be given with them and does it make them more effective?

Colleen Loo: Yes, in our trial that we are running, funded by the NHMRC, we
just have people on usually their stable doses of antidepressant medication, so
we give ketamine on top of that because there is no reason for stopping them,
but you're right, ketamine works on a different neurotransmitter system, different
chemicals in the brain, which is why it's a fascinating drug, and which probably
explains why it works so differently. You don't normally expect to see a rapid
response a day after starting an antidepressant medication.

Norman Swan: So briefly then, if somebody has got severe treatment resistant
depression and your doctor wants to give you a single dose of ketamine, that's
probably evidence-based but you're potentially getting into tiger country with
repeated doses and hold off until you know what the results of your trial is.

Colleen Loo: Exactly. So our trial is looking at the efficacy and safety of
repeated dosing. It looks at a four-week dosing protocol. It's a double-blind trial
but also with an open label treatment so that you can go on to have active
treatment. And I'm really interested beyond that in getting funding to look at what
a six-month treatment protocol should look like, because I think that's the ultimate
aim; how can we make this a clinically useful treatment?

Norman Swan: We'll book a slot for you to get the results on the Health Report.
Thanks for joining us Colleen.

Colleen Loo: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Professor Colleen Loo, who is Professor of Psychiatry at the
University of New South Wales and the Black Dog Institute.

Norman Swan: One in 200 Australian children live with epilepsy, four people in
100 will be diagnosed with epilepsy during their lives, and no doubt when you
hear the word epilepsy you think of a grand mal seizure where someone falls to
the ground, going stiff and blue and then jerking violently. But epilepsy is often far
more subtle and complicated and not always easy to diagnose and understand,
which makes it even more astounding that two-thirds of people labelled as having
epilepsy are not referred to an epilepsy specialist. All these are among the
reasons that the way the different types of epilepsy should be classified has had
its first revision in 30 years. One of the experts behind this is Professor Ingrid
Scheffer who is a paediatric neurologist and epileptologist at the University of

Melbourne, and co-winner of the Prime Minister's Science Prize in 2014 for her
work on epilepsy. Welcome Ingrid.

Ingrid Scheffer: Thank you very much, Norman.

Norman Swan: So suffice it to say this is complicated, we don't have three
years, we have about seven minutes. Just tell us, why the reclassification and
what's the net effect of it?

Ingrid Scheffer: Well, it was a desperate need to bring it up to date. Science has
moved on, epilepsy has moved on since 1989 and we needed to bring in their
new concepts to how we look at patients, how we make diagnoses, how we look
for causes, very importantly, and that of course influences treatment. So it was
very timely, but it is complex. And as Einstein said, it should be as simple as
possible but no simpler, and that was something we really struggled with, was
trying to get it so that it was using words that mean what they say and would be
something that patients could use, doctors could use and everyone around them.

Norman Swan: And you say in your paper that the science is not yet up to a
proper classification, that you can't classify it like cancer or diabetes, so you just
take a practical approach, an operational approach rather than a science-based
approach.

Ingrid Scheffer: Yes, but there's a lot more science informing it now than 30
years ago, and that of course will change dramatically in the next 10 or 20 years.

Norman Swan: So take us through some of the big changes.

Ingrid Scheffer: Well, I think the big changes are the framework for how we
approach…when you see somebody with their first seizure or in fact epilepsy if
it's uncontrolled, and first you want to know the type of seizure they have, so we
have a whole new framework of new terms for seizures which are meant to be
more transparent. And then we take them up to try to diagnose their epilepsy
type, and ideally their epilepsy syndrome. You can't always make a syndrome
diagnosis.

Norman Swan: By syndrome you mean what?

Ingrid Scheffer: By syndrome I mean types of seizures that might occur
together. So people will often have three or four different types of seizures and
you need to know what goes with what. And then the EEG or the brainwave
tracing, what that shows, and then maybe the MRI as well, and you put that all
together to make an epilepsy syndrome diagnosis. And a good example is
childhood absence epilepsy, where a child stops and stares.

Norman Swan: So take us through the classical types of epileptic seizures or fits
and what they look like and how it changes.

Ingrid Scheffer: Okay, well, the seizure types don't change, but the words have
improved. So you have two big groups where they begin in one part of the brain
which were called partial and are now called focal. And in focal seizures, which
are 60% of all epilepsy, so the biggest group, you can be with it, which we call an
aware seizure now…

Norman Swan: So you know you are having it.

Ingrid Scheffer: Exactly.

Norman Swan: Which when I was a medical student that told you it wasn't
epilepsy at all but now we know it is.

Ingrid Scheffer: Exactly. And now impaired awareness. So instead of what was
complex partial, and complex doesn't mean not knowing where you are but
impaired awareness does, so now it's focal impaired awareness seizure. That's
diagnosis is critical, if you have it you can't drive, so it's a really important one for
our society.

Norman Swan: So it has an impact. And these focal epilepsies, they can be an
unusual behaviour, you stand up and walk to the end of the room and you don't
know where you are when you come round.

Ingrid Scheffer: Exactly, so you can just be a bit confused, 'off the air' we often
say, you might look to one side, you might go pale, you might do nothing, it can
be really boring to look at.

Norman Swan: So in the old days this was what was called petit mal, is it?

Ingrid Scheffer: Well, that's the problem with the French, everyone loves the
petit mal and the grand mal, but in fact they meant a host of different seizure
types, so they went out in 1981.

Norman Swan: All right, that shows how up-to-date I am.

Ingrid Scheffer: And we've now been working on these other ones. So there's a
focal group, and then the other big group are the generalised groups, which start
in both sides of the brain at once and involve the old grand mal means tonic
clonic, where you go stiff, tonic, and clonic, jerking, so stiffen and jerking, and
you fall to the ground with loss of consciousness. And the other main well-known
ones are absence, so you stop and stare, often just for five seconds and then
you are back with it. And the third big one is the myoclonic seizure where you
jerk.

Norman Swan: So then go down a level, so that's, if you like, exactly what is
happening to you and describing it for what it is. The causes…the reason you
and Sam Berkovic got the PM's Science Prize was for your work on the genetics
of this.

Ingrid Scheffer: Exactly, so the causes are now up front and centre. From the
moment you see somebody with a seizure you have to ask yourself what's the
cause. And when we started in what we are doing there were no genes known
for epilepsy, we found the first one in 1995 with John Mulley from Adelaide. And
that really has made…genetics has since come to the fore with new next-
generation sequencing techniques, the new gene finding science, and we now
have about 400 genes known for epilepsy, so there are many.

Norman Swan: Mostly in childhood epilepsy or first seizure in adults? Because
the first seizure in adults the alarm bells ring; does this person have a malignant
tumour, for example, what's going on here?

Ingrid Scheffer: So more in childhood and adolescent onset, but some adults
can have genetic forms as well. And they may have malformations, and we know
that there are subtle malformations of the brain that cause focal epilepsies, but
there's a whole host of other causes that we now think about, including structural
changes and metabolic changes.

Norman Swan: Where can people go to find out more?

Ingrid Scheffer: Well, the International League Against Epilepsy is the
international body that defines epilepsy, and this is like the DSM5, if you like,
which is for psychiatry but the equivalent for epilepsy, and so you can look at
their website to get more information.

Norman Swan: And get a referral to an epileptologist rather than sticking with
the doctor who doesn't necessarily…

Ingrid Scheffer: Oh I think lots of paediatricians and neurologists are very
capable with epilepsy, so they'd be perfectly good too.

Norman Swan: Ingrid Scheffer, thanks for joining us.

Ingrid Scheffer: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Professor Ingrid Scheffer is a paediatric neurologist and
epileptoloist at the University of Melbourne.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report, and I hope you can join me
next week.
